title: A Spacecraft Took a Selfie with Mars — and Caught a Secret in the Video!
summary: Imagine you're on a road trip across the solar system, and you get to swing by Mars for a speed boost! That's exactly what NASA's Psyche spacecraft did on May 15. It flew past the Red Planet, using Mars's gravity like a slingshot to zoom faster toward its real target: a mysterious asteroid named Psyche. This asteroid is special — it's made mostly of metal, like the core of a planet that never finished forming. Psyche will reach it in 2029. But the flyby wasn't just for speed. It was a chance to test the spacecraft's science tools. One tool, a neutron detector, felt neutrons escaping from Mars's surface. Neutrons are tiny particles that can tell us what a planet is made of. The detector worked perfectly! Another tool, a magnetometer, measured Mars's magnetic field. As Psyche flew through a shockwave where solar wind slams into the planet, the magnetometer recorded a big jump in magnetism. The coolest part? Two cameras took over a month of photos and made a time-lapse video. At first, Mars looked like a thin crescent. Then we saw craters, the south polar ice cap, and a huge double-ringed crater called Huygens. The cameras even spotted Mars's two moons, Phobos and Deimos, from super far away — like finding a firefly in a football stadium! This practice will help scientists search for tiny moons around asteroid Psyche later. All the tools passed their tests with flying colors. Now Psyche is racing toward the asteroid belt, ready to uncover secrets of a metal world.
why_it_matters: When scientists test space tools on real planets today, they are learning how to explore new places tomorrow — maybe even finding out what the core of our own Earth looks like.

background_read: NASA's Psyche spacecraft launched in 2023 on a SpaceX rocket from Florida. It will travel for six years to reach the asteroid Psyche, which orbits the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.
The asteroid was discovered in 1852 and is thought to be the leftover metal core of an early planet. Scientists have never visited a metal world before.

During the flyby, Psyche used Mars’s gravity to change its path and pick up speed, a move called a gravity assist. Many deep-space missions, like Voyager and Cassini, have used this same clever trick.
Article_Structure: WHAT: Flew by Mars, tested its science tools, and made a time-lapse video of the planet and its moons
WHY: To gain speed toward the asteroid Psyche and to test cameras and detectors for the future mission

perspectives.description: All the tools passed their tests perfectly, so the team is very happy. This success means the spacecraft is ready to study the metal asteroid.
Some people say that sending robots to asteroids is very expensive, and that money could be used to fix problems here on Earth first.
Many people are fascinated by Psyche because no one has ever seen a metal asteroid up close. They wonder what secrets it holds about how planets are built.
